opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something I think about a lot, because there's a natural tension there. The semantic web vision, with RDF triples, ontologies, and carefully curated schemas, is in some sense the ancestor of what we're doing. HippoRAG also builds a graph of entities and relations. But we made a pretty deliberate choice to go schemaless. We use an LLM to do open information extraction, pulling out noun phrases and relations as they appear in the text, without forcing them into a predefined ontology.

The reason is that the hippocampal indexing analogy we started from isn't really about having a perfectly organized, canonical representation of the world. It's about having a flexible index of associations that can be built quickly from raw experience and then traversed to pull in related memories. Personalized PageRank over a messy, open graph turns out to be surprisingly good at that. You don't need the graph to be correct in a formal logical sense. You need it to connect the right things.

So my view is that the path toward the semantic web shouldn't be "replace the open graph with a strict ontology." It should be more of a layering. Where good structured knowledge already exists, things like Wikidata or domain ontologies in biomedicine, you should be able to link your extracted entities to those canonical nodes. That gives you better entity resolution, which is honestly one of the weakest points in an open KG approach. You get a lot of near-duplicate nodes, synonyms, and inconsistent relation phrasings, and grounding them against a shared vocabulary helps clean that up. It also makes knowledge shareable across corpora and across systems, which is really the core promise of the semantic web.

But I'd want to keep the open, schemaless layer underneath, because the real world, and especially the long tail of what people actually want to retrieve, doesn't fit neatly into anyone's ontology. New concepts show up all the time. If everything has to pass through a schema before it can be remembered, you lose exactly the kind of fast, continual learning we were trying to get at.

So I'd describe it as a hybrid: an associative, LLM-built memory that's opportunistically anchored to structured, shared knowledge where that exists. And then there are open research questions. How do you decide when two extracted entities should be merged with a canonical node? How do you handle conflicting or time-varying facts? How do you let the structure evolve as the system learns, rather than freezing it? I think those are much more interesting problems than just picking a format, and they're where I'd like to see the work go.

r001.rationale: The response recommends linking extracted entities to structured knowledge while retaining a schemaless layer, but it does not say to first establish whether HippoRAG generalizes at medium scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because in some sense HippoRAG is already a step in that direction, even if we didn't frame it that way at first. The knowledge graph we build is essentially a very loose, very noisy semantic web. We take passages, we run open information extraction with an LLM, we get these subject-predicate-object triples, and we link the nodes with synonymy edges from the embedding model. It's a schema-free graph, which is exactly what made it easy to build at scale, but it's also exactly what makes it fall short of what people traditionally mean by a semantic web.

So I think the path forward has a few stages. The first is that we need to get more structure without losing the flexibility. Right now a node is just a string, "Barack Obama" or "Stanford," and the relations are whatever the LLM decided to write. If you look at classical semantic web work, the whole point is that entities have types, relations have well-defined semantics, and you can do things like reasoning over an ontology. We don't want to go all the way back to hand-crafted ontologies, because that's what failed to scale in the first place, but I think there's a middle ground where the LLM proposes a lightweight schema as it reads, and the graph gradually becomes more canonical. The synonymy edges are a crude version of that already. The next version is actual entity resolution and relation normalization that's done continuously, not just at retrieval time.

The second stage is interoperability. One of the most exciting things about the semantic web vision was that you could link your graph to someone else's graph, to Wikidata, to a company's internal knowledge base, and the retrieval would just work across them. HippoRAG's retrieval is Personalized PageRank over the graph, and PageRank doesn't actually care where the nodes came from. So if we can get the schema alignment right, you could plug in an existing structured knowledge base as a set of nodes and edges, and the LLM-extracted graph from unstructured text becomes the glue that connects it to the long tail of information that was never curated. I think that's really the dream: structured knowledge where it exists, LLM-extracted knowledge where it doesn't, and one retrieval process over both.

The third thing, and this is where I think the neuroscience framing is actually still useful, is that the graph should be allowed to be wrong and to change. The hippocampal index in the brain is not a clean database, it's constantly being updated and reconsolidated. A semantic web built by LLMs will have extraction errors, it'll have contradictions, and the system needs a way to handle that gracefully rather than treating every triple as ground truth. So I'd like to see confidence scores on edges, provenance that points back to the source passage, and some mechanism where repeated retrieval or new evidence can strengthen or weaken connections over time.

And then honestly the last piece is evaluation. Multi-hop QA benchmarks like MuSiQue and HotpotQA were great for showing that the graph structure helps with associativity, but they don't really test whether you're building something that behaves like a usable knowledge base. We'd need tasks that reward consistency, that reward being able to answer questions you weren't explicitly trained on, and that penalize hallucinated structure. So if I had to summarize it, I'd say: keep the LLM as the extractor because that's what solves the scaling problem, add just enough schema that the graph can talk to other graphs, make the whole thing updatable and uncertain rather than static, and then build benchmarks that actually measure whether it's working as a semantic web and not just as a retriever.

r001.rationale: The response recommends adding schema, interoperability, and evaluation, but does not call for first establishing whether HippoRAG generalizes at medium scale before semantic-web integration.

astra-6.text:
I think a promising direction is to treat the semantic web as an additional source of structure for HippoRAG. When you build a graph from text, you have to resolve things like whether two mentions refer to the same entity and what a relationship actually means. An existing knowledge graph could help ground those decisions and connect information across documents.

But I wouldn’t make a complete semantic web a prerequisite. I’d start with a domain where we have both documents and a reasonably good ontology, connect the extracted graph to that ontology, and test whether it improves retrieval—especially for questions that require connecting several pieces of evidence. We’d also want to preserve the links back to the original passages, so you can inspect what supports an answer.

So I’d approach it incrementally: use existing semantic structure where it helps, keep the flexibility to incorporate new information from text, and let retrieval quality guide how much structure we introduce.

r001.rationale: The response recommends an incremental ontology-based trial and testing retrieval quality, but does not say to establish HippoRAG’s medium-scale generalization before semantic web integration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step is to move toward a richer, more interconnected representation of knowledge. In HippoRAG, we use a knowledge graph to connect information across passages, so retrieval can follow relationships that a purely similarity-based search might miss. A semantic web could extend that idea beyond the graph built from a particular collection of documents.

But I would approach it incrementally. You need to resolve when two sources are talking about the same entity, preserve where each claim came from, and handle conflicting information. Simply connecting more things doesn’t necessarily make retrieval better; it can introduce noise.

So I’d start by linking our graphs to existing structured knowledge and measuring whether those connections actually help answer questions that require combining information across sources. The goal would be a system that can use both the structure of the graph and the meaning of the original text, without losing the evidence behind an answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends incremental linking to structured knowledge and measuring its impact, but does not say to establish HippoRAG’s medium-scale generalization before semantic-web integration.
